topics.title: Trigonometric Identities & Values
topics.notes:
1. Core Trigonometric Identities

Pythagorean identities form the absolute bedrock of trigonometric simplification. In both the CDS and NDA exams, UPSC rarely asks direct identity questions; instead, they embed these identities into complex algebraic expressions, quadratic equations, or calculus integrations. Master these variations:

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
    • Exam Manipulation: $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta = (1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \cos\theta)$
    • Exam Manipulation: $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta = (1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)$
  • sec²θ - tan²θ = 1 (valid for $\theta \neq (2n+1)\pi/2$)
    • Exam Manipulation: $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ ; $\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta - 1$
    • ⚠️ Critical UPSC Shortcut: Since $a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)$, we get: $$\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta + \tan\theta}$$ UPSC frequently sets up questions where $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = k$, meaning you must instantly deduce that $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac{1}{k}$ to solve for $\sec\theta$ or $\tan\theta$.
  • cosec²θ - cot²θ = 1 (valid for $\theta \neq n\pi$)
    • Exam Manipulation: $\csc^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\theta$ ; $\cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta - 1$
    • ⚠️ Critical UPSC Shortcut: Similarly: $$\csc\theta - \cot\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta + \cot\theta}$$ If $\csc\theta + \cot\theta = p$, then $\csc\theta - \cot\theta = \frac{1}{p}$.
💡 Fun Fact time!
Did you know that the reciprocal identity trick $(\sec\theta - \tan\theta) = 1/(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)$ was the star of a highly tricky question in the recent NDA papers? UPSC gave $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 4$ and asked for the value of $\sin\theta$. By instantly writing $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = 1/4$, students could add the two equations to get $2\sec\theta = 17/4 \implies \cos\theta = 8/17$, leading directly to the Pythagorean triplet $(8, 15, 17)$ and $\sin\theta = 15/17$ in under 30 seconds!

2. Sum & Difference Formulas

Used to resolve non-standard angles (like $15^\circ$, $75^\circ$, $105^\circ$) into standard values. UPSC expects you to have these memorized and to recognize them in reverse order to simplify long chains of trigonometric terms:

  • $\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B$
  • $\cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B$ (Note the sign reversal!)
  • $\tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A \tan B}$
  • $\cot(A \pm B) = \frac{\cot A \cot B \mp 1}{cot B \pm \cot A}$
💡 Memory Hack!
To remember the sign conventions of compound formulas:
• Sine is "Social": It mixes terms ($\sin \cos$) and keeps the original sign ($+$ stays $+$, $-$ stays $-$).
• Cosine is "Selfish": It groups its own terms ($\cos \cos$ and $\sin \sin$) and always changes the sign ($+$ becomes $-$, $-$ becomes $+$).

3. Multiple Angle Identities

Essential for reducing powers of trigonometric functions. NDA calculus problems (differentiation and integration) rely heavily on these to make expressions solvable:

  • $\sin 2A = 2 \sin A \cos A = \frac{2\tan A}{1 + \tan^2 A}$
  • $\cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A = \frac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A}$
    Exam Warning: Always look out for $1 - \cos 2A = 2\sin^2 A$ and $1 + \cos 2A = 2\cos^2 A$. These are the most highly exploited substitutions in the calculus segment of the NDA.
  • $\tan 2A = \frac{2\tan A}{1 - \tan^2 A}$
  • $\sin 3A = 3\sin A - 4\sin^3 A$
  • $\cos 3A = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A$
  • $\tan 3A = \frac{3\tan A - \tan^3 A}{1 - 3\tan^2 A}$

4. Product-to-Sum & Sum-to-Product

These formulas act as translation keys. UPSC examiners love to test your ability to convert a product series (which is hard to integrate or simplify) into a sum series (which is easy to manage):

  • $2 \sin A \cos B = \sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)$
  • $2 \cos A \sin B = \sin(A + B) - \sin(A - B)$
  • $2 \cos A \cos B = \cos(A + B) + \cos(A - B)$
  • $2 \sin A \sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)$ (Watch out for the reversed order of angles!)
  • $\sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$
  • $\sin C - \sin D = 2 \cos\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$
  • $\cos C + \cos D = 2 \cos\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$
  • $\cos C - \cos D = -2 \sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$ or $2 \sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{D-C}{2}\right)$
[ Advanced Revision Data ]

Trigonometric Identities & Values

Trigonometry, derived from the Greek words 'trigonon' (triangle) and 'metron' (measure), is the study of relationships between side lengths and angles of triangles. For defense aspirants, this is not just theoretical math—it is the foundational science powering missile ballistics, radar coordinates, sonar depth calculations, and flight path navigation. This section consolidates the exact algebraic relationships and specific values that UPSC tests on a standard pattern.

1. Angle Measurement Systems

UPSC often blends degree and radian measures within a single question to catch students who fail to convert units before applying formulas.

  • Degree Measure (Sexagesimal System): A complete rotation is divided into 360 degrees ($360^\circ$). Each degree is subdivided into 60 minutes ($60'$) and each minute into 60 seconds ($60''$).
  • Radian Measure (Circular System): The standard unit of angular measure in calculus. One radian is the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle. A complete revolution is $2\pi$ radians.
Feature Degree Measure (Sexagesimal) Radian Measure (Circular)
Full Circle $360^\circ$ $2\pi \text{ rad}$
Conversion Factor $D = R \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ $R = D \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ}$
Base Equivalences $1^\circ \approx 0.01745 \text{ rad}$ $1 \text{ rad} \approx 57^\circ 16' 22''$
UPSC Trap Focus Avoid mixing: $\sin(1^\circ)$ is vastly different from $\sin(1 \text{ rad})$ because $1 \text{ rad} \approx 57^\circ$. Note: $\sin(1) > \sin(1^\circ)$. In limit problems and calculus, angles MUST be in Radians. Never use degrees in derivative formulas!

2. Basic Trigonometric Ratios

For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle, the six trigonometric ratios are absolute:

  • $\sin \theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}$
  • $\cos \theta = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}$
  • $\tan \theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Adjacent}} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \quad (\theta \neq (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2})$
  • $\csc \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta} = \frac{\text{Hypotenuse}}{\text{Opposite}} \quad (\theta \neq n\pi)$
  • $\sec \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta} = \frac{\text{Hypotenuse}}{\text{Adjacent}} \quad (\theta \neq (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2})$
  • $\cot \theta = \frac{1}{\tan \theta} = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Opposite}} \quad (\theta \neq n\pi)$
UPSC Domain Warning: When evaluating trigonometric functions, always pay attention to values where the functions are undefined. UPSC regularly constructs statements like: "The equation $\sec\theta = x$ has solutions for all real numbers." This is false, because the range of $\sec\theta$ (and $\csc\theta$) is $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$. The values between $-1$ and $1$ are excluded!

3. Trigonometric Values for Standard & Non-Standard Angles

Having standard angles memorized is a prerequisite. To gain a true competitive edge in CDS and NDA, you must also memorize the non-standard values shown beneath this table:

Angle ($\theta$) $0^\circ$ ($0$ rad) $30^\circ$ ($\pi/6$ rad) $45^\circ$ ($\pi/4$ rad) $60^\circ$ ($\pi/3$ rad) $90^\circ$ ($\pi/2$ rad)
$\sin \theta$ $0$ $1/2$ $1/\sqrt{2}$ $\sqrt{3}/2$ $1$
$\cos \theta$ $1$ $\sqrt{3}/2$ $1/\sqrt{2}$ $1/2$ $0$
$\tan \theta$ $0$ $1/\sqrt{3}$ $1$ $\sqrt{3}$ Undefined

💡 Premium UPSC Value Vault (Memorize these!):

  • $\sin 15^\circ = \cos 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2\sqrt{2}}$
  • $\cos 15^\circ = \sin 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$
  • $\tan 15^\circ = \cot 75^\circ = 2 - \sqrt{3}$
  • $\tan 75^\circ = \cot 15^\circ = 2 + \sqrt{3}$
  • $\sin 18^\circ = \cos 72^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}$ (Highly recurring!)
  • $\cos 36^\circ = \sin 54^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{4}$

4. Signs of Trigonometric Ratios in Quadrants (CAST Rule)

An angle’s position in the Cartesian plane dictates its sign. Misapplying quadrant signs is the number one source of negative marking in the NDA exam.

💡 Memory Hack!
Remember the quadrant signs using the sequence I ➔ II ➔ III ➔ IV:
Add Sugar To Coffee
• All positive in Quadrant I ($0$ to $\pi/2$)
• Sine (and $\csc$) positive in Quadrant II ($\pi/2$ to $\pi$)
• Tangent (and $\cot$) positive in Quadrant III ($\pi$ to $3\pi/2$)
• Cosine (and $\sec$) positive in Quadrant IV ($3\pi/2$ to $2\pi$)

5. Trigonometric Ratios of Allied Angles

Allied angles are angles of the form $(n \cdot 90^\circ \pm \theta)$ or $(n \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} \pm \theta)$. Use these two rules to never make a mistake again:

  1. The Function Switch Rule:
    • If $n$ is even (e.g., $180^\circ$, $360^\circ$, $\pi$, $2\pi$), the function remains unchanged ($\sin \to \sin$, $\cos \to \cos$).
    • If $n$ is odd (e.g., $90^\circ$, $270^\circ$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$), the function changes to its co-function ($\sin \leftrightarrow \cos$, $\tan \leftrightarrow \cot$, $\sec \leftrightarrow \csc$).
  2. The Sign Rule: The sign of the output depends on the quadrant of the original function.
Function Type Behavior with Negative Input $f(-\theta)$ Trigonometric Functions
Odd Functions $f(-\theta) = -f(\theta)$
(The negative sign "spits out")		 $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$
$\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta$
$\csc(-\theta) = -\csc\theta$
$\cot(-\theta) = -\cot\theta$
Even Functions $f(-\theta) = f(\theta)$
(The negative sign is absorbed)		 $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$
$\sec(-\theta) = \sec\theta$
💡 Fun Fact time!
The even/odd properties of trigonometric functions are highly tested in NDA's calculus section, especially in Definite Integration. Whenever you see a symmetric interval like $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx$, check if $f(x)$ is odd. If the function contains an odd term like $\sin^3 x \cdot \cos^2 x$, the integral instantly evaluates to $0$ without any manual integration. A massive time saver!

6. Conditional Identities (Crucial for Triangle-Based Questions)

In any triangle $ABC$ (where $A+B+C = \pi$ or $180^\circ$):

  • $\sin 2A + \sin 2B + \sin 2C = 4 \sin A \sin B \sin C$
  • $\sin A + \sin B + \sin C = 4 \cos \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{C}{2}$
  • $\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A \tan B \tan C$ (Extremely high-yield in CDS!)
  • $\cot A \cot B + \cot B \cot C + \cot C \cot A = 1$

7. Common Traps & Exam Hacks to Avoid Negative Marks

  1. Treating Ratios Algebraically: Remember $(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2$ is NOT $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta$. It expands to $1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1 + \sin 2\theta$. This identity is highly useful in simplifying radical forms like $\sqrt{1 + \sin 2\theta} = |\sin\theta + \cos\theta|$.
  2. Neglecting Quadrant Domains: When taking the square root of a trigonometric identity, write it as absolute values. For example, $\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} = |\sin\theta|$. If the question states that $\theta$ lies in Quadrant III, then $|\sin\theta| = -\sin\theta$.
  3. Confusing Inverse Notation: Remember that $\sin^{-1}x \neq \frac{1}{\sin x}$. The notation $\sin^{-1}x$ denotes the arc-sine function, whereas $(\sin x)^{-1}$ denotes $\csc x$.

8. Shortcuts & Tricks: The Value Substitution Technique

If a question consists of a complex trigonometric expression and the options are independent of $\theta$ (i.e., they are constant numbers like $0, 1, 2, -1$), do not simplify the identity algebraically!
Simply substitute a convenient standard angle for $\theta$ (such as $0^\circ, 45^\circ,$ or $90^\circ$) that does not make any term in the expression undefined.

  • Example: Evaluate $\cos^6\theta + \sin^6\theta + 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$.
  • Substitution Hack: Put $\theta = 0^\circ \implies \cos(0) = 1, \sin(0) = 0$.
  • Result: $1^6 + 0^6 + 3(0)(1) = 1$. The answer is instantly found without algebraic expansion!

topics.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
topics.notes:
1. Principal Value Branches (PVB)

The domain and range must be strictly memorized to solve standard NDA/CDS equations. In recent UPSC papers, the examiners deliberately frame questions using angles outside the principal value range to trap students who use mechanical cancellations (like blindly writing $\sin^{-1}(\sin \theta) = \theta$).

💡 Memory Hack!
Divide the six functions into two distinct "Families" to easily recall their Range (PVB):
  • The "S-Family" (Symmetric around Origin): $\sin^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$, and $\csc^{-1}$ live in the vertical zone of $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$. Mnemonic: "Sine's squad stands straight."
  • The "C-Family" (Continuous Positive Zone): $\cos^{-1}$, $\cot^{-1}$, and $\sec^{-1}$ live in the horizontal zone of $[0, \pi]$. Mnemonic: "Cosine's crew is completely positive."

To avoid silly mistakes on domain boundaries, always analyze the exact limits before attempting algebraic manipulations:

  • $\sin^{-1} x$ : Domain = $[-1, 1]$ , Range (PVB) = $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$
  • $\cos^{-1} x$ : Domain = $[-1, 1]$ , Range (PVB) = $[0, \pi]$
  • $\tan^{-1} x$ : Domain = $\mathbb{R}$ , Range (PVB) = $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$
  • $\csc^{-1} x$ : Domain = $\mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1)$ , Range (PVB) = $[-\pi/2, \pi/2] \setminus \{0\}$
  • $\sec^{-1} x$ : Domain = $\mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1)$ , Range (PVB) = $[0, \pi] \setminus \{\pi/2\}$
  • $\cot^{-1} x$ : Domain = $\mathbb{R}$ , Range (PVB) = $(0, \pi)$
💡 Fun Fact time!
In the 2024 NDA paper, UPSC tested candidates on $\sin^{-1}(\sin \theta)$ where $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{4}$. Students who blindly cancelled the functions to get $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ lost marks because $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ lies outside the range $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$. The correct approach is evaluating $\sin^{-1}(\sin(\pi - \frac{\pi}{4})) = \sin^{-1}(\sin \frac{\pi}{4}) = \frac{\pi}{4}$. Always check your boundaries!

2. Concept Comparison: The S-Family vs. The C-Family

NDA/CDS questions often mix properties of these two groups to construct complex identity-based equations. Study their structural differences below:

Feature The S-Family ($\sin^{-1} x, \tan^{-1} x, \csc^{-1} x$) The C-Family ($\cos^{-1} x, \cot^{-1} x, \sec^{-1} x$)
Behavior with Negative Input Odd Function Behavior:
$f(-x) = -f(x)$
Directly pulls the minus sign out.		 Symmetric Shift:
$f(-x) = \pi - f(x)$
Subtracts the value from $\pi$ to stay positive.
Principal Range Quadrants Quadrant I (for $x > 0$) &
Quadrant IV (for $x < 0$)		 Quadrant I (for $x > 0$) &
Quadrant II (for $x < 0$)
Symmetry on Graph Symmetric about the Origin Symmetric about the line $y = \pi/2$

3. Fundamental Properties & Algebraic Identities

  • $\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1} x$ , $\csc^{-1}(-x) = -\csc^{-1} x$ , $\tan^{-1}(-x) = -\tan^{-1} x$
  • $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x$ , $\sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1} x$ , $\cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1} x$
  • $\sin^{-1}(1/x) = \csc^{-1} x$ (for $|x| \ge 1$)
  • $\cos^{-1}(1/x) = \sec^{-1} x$ (for $|x| \ge 1$)
  • $\tan^{-1}(1/x) = \cot^{-1} x$ (for $x > 0$) [Warning: If $x < 0$, $\tan^{-1}(1/x) = -\pi + \cot^{-1} x$]

4. Complementary Angles & Multi-Angle Transformations

  • $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \pi/2$ (for $x \in [-1, 1]$)
  • $\tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \pi/2$ (for $x \in \mathbb{R}$)
  • $\csc^{-1} x + \sec^{-1} x = \pi/2$ (for $|x| \ge 1$)
  • $\tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - xy}\right)$ [if $xy < 1$]
  • $\tan^{-1} x - \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x - y}{1 + xy}\right)$ [if $xy > -1$]
  • $2\tan^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{1-x^2}\right)$
[ Advanced Revision Data ]

Inverse Trigonometric Functions – Advanced Calculus & System Solvability

1. Formal Definition & Principal Value Branches

The inverse trigonometric functions are the set of functions that reverse the action of the six elementary trigonometric functions on a restricted domain so that each becomes one‑to‑one. For a given trigonometric function $f$, its inverse is denoted by $f^{-1}$ (e.g., $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$). The restriction is called the principal value branch and is chosen to make the inverse single‑valued.

Principal Value Ranges
Inverse Domain Range (Principal Value)
$\sin^{-1} x$ $-1\le x\le 1$ $[-\frac{\pi}{2},\;\frac{\pi}{2}]$
$\cos^{-1} x$ $-1\le x\le 1$ $[0,\;\pi]$
$\tan^{-1} x$ $-\infty < x < \infty$ $(-\frac{\pi}{2},\;\frac{\pi}{2})$
$\cot^{-1} x$ $-\infty < x < \infty$ $(0,\;\pi)$
$\sec^{-1} x$ $|x|\ge 1$ $[0,\;\pi]\setminus\{\frac{\pi}{2}\}$
$\csc^{-1} x$ $|x|\ge 1$ $[-\frac{\pi}{2},\;\frac{\pi}{2}]\setminus\{0\}$

2. Fundamental Identities Derived from Definitions

Starting from the definition $y=\sin^{-1}x \iff \sin y=x$ with $y\in[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}]$, we can obtain key identities that are indispensable in solving NDA / CDS algebraic systems:

  • Reciprocal Relations
    • $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, valid for $x\in[-1,1]$.
    • $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, valid for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
    • $\sec^{-1}x+\csc^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, valid for $|x|\ge 1$.
  • Double‑Angle Transformations
    • $\sin^{-1}x=2\sin^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{x}{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\Big)$, for $|x|\le 1$.
    • $\tan^{-1}x=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}\Big)$, for $x\neq\pm1$.

3. Derivatives & Integrals – Analytical Formulation

Using implicit differentiation on the defining equation $\sin y=x$, we establish the exact rates of change:

Derivative of $\sin^{-1}x$:

$$\frac{d}{dx}\big(\sin^{-1}x\big)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}},\qquad |x|<1$$

Analogously, the other derivatives are:

  • $\frac{d}{dx}\big(\cos^{-1}x\big)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}},\qquad |x|<1$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\big(\tan^{-1}x\big)=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\big(\cot^{-1}x\big)=-\frac{1}{1+x^{2}},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\big(\sec^{-1}x\big)=\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2}-1}},\qquad |x|>1$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\big(\csc^{-1}x\big)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2}-1}},\qquad |x|>1$

Integration formulas that frequently appear in NDA calculus sections:

  • $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}x+C$
  • $\int \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}=\tan^{-1}x+C$
  • $\int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}=\sec^{-1}|x|+C$ (for $|x|>1$)
💡 Fun Fact time!
The derivative of $\tan^{-1}x$ is one of the most frequently targeted forms in NDA integration questions. UPSC often hides this under a substitution format, such as integrating $\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^2}$. Recognizing that $dt = \frac{dx}{1+x^2}$ transforms the entire problem into a simple $\int e^t dt$ step!

4. Composite Angles and Substitution Forms

When the argument of an inverse function is a rational expression, you can convert it to a standard angle using addition formulas:

$$\sin^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}\Big)=2\theta,\qquad -\frac{\pi}{4}<\theta<\frac{\pi}{4}$$

Similarly:

$$\tan^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}\Big)=\alpha,\qquad -\frac{\pi}{2}<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}$$

5. Table of Standard Angles

Argument $\sin^{-1}$ $\cos^{-1}$ $\tan^{-1}$
$0$ $0$ $\frac{\pi}{2}$ $0$
$1$ $\frac{\pi}{2}$ $0$ $\frac{\pi}{4}$
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\frac{\pi}{8}$ (Using identities)
$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\frac{\pi}{3}$ $\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\frac{\pi}{3}$
$-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $-\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ $-\frac{\pi}{4}$

6. Graphical Characteristics (Qualitative Analysis)

  • All six inverse trigonometric functions are continuous and monotonic on their restricted principal domains.
  • $\sin^{-1} x$ is strictly increasing on $[-1,1]$.
  • $\cos^{-1} x$ is strictly decreasing on $[-1,1]$.
  • $\tan^{-1} x$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$, bounded by horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.

7. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Ignoring Principal Value Restrictions – Students often apply $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)=\theta$ without checking whether $\theta$ lies inside $[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}]$.
  • Sign Errors in Derivatives – The derivative of $\cos^{-1}x$ is negative; forgetting the minus sign leads to incorrect integration.
  • Mis-using Reciprocal Identities – Treating $\sec^{-1}x$ as $1/\cos^{-1}x$ is structurally incorrect; the correct relation is $\sec^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}\!\big(\frac{1}{x}\big)$ with domain $|x|\ge1$.
  • Omitting Absolute Values – In the derivative of $\sec^{-1}x$, the factor $|x|$ in the denominator is crucial; omitting it gives sign errors for negative $x$.

8. Shortcuts & Quick-Solver Tricks

  • Use the "Sum‑to‑Product" Inverse Trick: $$\sin^{-1}a+\sin^{-1}b=\sin^{-1}\!\Big(a\sqrt{1-b^{2}}+b\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\Big)$$ when $a^{2}+b^{2} \le 1$ or if $ab < 0$.
  • Rapid Conversion between $\tan^{-1}$ and $\sin^{-1}$: $$\tan^{-1}x=\sin^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\Big)$$ This is useful when evaluating trigonometric composite terms.

9. Worked Example 1 – Evaluating a Complex Inverse Sum

Problem: Find the exact value of $S=\sin^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{3}{5}\Big)+\cos^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{4}{5}\Big)$.

Solution Steps:

  1. Recognize that if $x = \frac{3}{5}$, then $\sqrt{1-x^2} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{4}{5}$.
  2. Using the complementary identity: $\sin^{-1}y + \cos^{-1}y = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Let's rewrite $\cos^{-1}(\frac{4}{5})$ in terms of sine.
  3. Let $\theta = \cos^{-1}(\frac{4}{5}) \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \frac{4}{5} \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{3}{5} \Rightarrow \theta = \sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5})$.
  4. Thus, $\cos^{-1}(\frac{4}{5}) = \sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5})$.
  5. We can now substitute: $S = \sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) + \sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) = 2\sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5})$.
  6. Alternatively, since $\sin^{-1}(x) = \cos^{-1}(\sqrt{1-x^2})$ for $x > 0$, we have $\sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) = \cos^{-1}(\frac{4}{5})$. Substituting this gives $\sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) + \cos^{-1}(\frac{4}{5}) = \sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) + \sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5})$ or simply evaluate using the complementary relationship if the arguments were complementary (e.g., $\sin^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) + \cos^{-1}(\frac{3}{5}) = \frac{\pi}{2}$). Since the arguments are different, we use our substitution to get: $2 \sin^{-1}(0.6) \approx 1.287\text{ rad}$.

10. Worked Example 2 – Solving an Equation Involving $\tan^{-1}$ (UPSC Style)

Problem: Determine the number of real solutions for $x$ in: $$\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{1}{x}\Big)=\frac{\pi}{4}.$$

Solution Steps:

  1. Recall the piecewise property of reciprocal inverse tangents: $$\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{1}{x}\Big)=\begin{cases} \frac{\pi}{2}, & x>0\\[4pt] -\frac{\pi}{2}, & x<0 \end{cases}$$
  2. The given equation states that the sum of these two terms must equal $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
  3. However, by analytical definition, the sum can only be $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (for positive real $x$) or $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ (for negative real $x$).
  4. Since $\frac{\pi}{4}$ is neither $\frac{\pi}{2}$ nor $-\frac{\pi}{2}$, there are no real values of $x$ that can satisfy this equation.
  5. Thus, the number of real solutions is $\mathbf{0}$ (Empty set $\varnothing$).

11. Advanced Result – Inverse Function Composition

For composite forms like $\sin^{-1}(\cos\theta)$, we convert using the identity $\cos\theta=\sin\!\big(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\big)$ and then apply the principal range:

$$\sin^{-1}(\cos\theta)=\sin^{-1}\!\Big(\sin\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\big)\Big)=\begin{cases} \tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta, & -\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}\\[4pt] \theta-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, & \frac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le\frac{3\pi}{2} \end{cases}$$

12. Summary of Key Formulas

  • $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$
  • $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$
  • $\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}x=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$
  • $\tan^{-1}x=\sin^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\Big)$
  • $\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{a+b}{1-ab}\Big)$ (for $ab < 1$)
⚡ High-Yield Exam Facts (NDA/CDS/AFCAT)
  • $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \pi/2$ holds strictly for $x \in [-1, 1]$. UPSC frequently tests this boundary condition.
  • $\tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1}(1/x)$ is piecewise constant. It is $\pi/2$ for positive $x$ and $-\pi/2$ for negative $x$.
  • Derivative relations are a frequent shortcut in calculus. $\frac{d}{dx} [\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x] = 0$ because the sum is a constant ($\pi/2$).
  • Always keep angles in radians. NDA options are systematically framed in radians; degree answers are intentionally put as decoy choices.
